prize_parts.citation: For the invention of the optical lattice clock, based on trapping many atoms at a magic wavelength, and its realisation at the 10^-18 level of accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single-part prize for optical lattice clocks, credited to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. The chair asked us to test the case on its own evidence and not on the opening ranking, so I have done that. The central idea is physical, not a refinement: choose the trapping wavelength so that the light shift is identical for both clock states, and thousands of atoms can be held for long interrogation times with Doppler and recoil shifts suppressed and the clock transition left undisturbed. This is distinct from a single trapped ion, where a Paul trap and quantum logic do the work and the statistics are limited by one particle, and distinct from the comb, which is a ruler and not the reference. The consequence is an instrument whose independent realisations at several national laboratories agree near 1e-18, and which resolves the gravitational redshift over millimetre-scale height differences in the laboratory. That last point is what keeps me from calling it mere engineering: general relativity is being read off a table-top device. Attribution is compact, which I value more as Secretary the longer I see the alternatives. Katori proposed the lattice and made the first strontium demonstrations; Ye's group carried it to record accuracy and stability and into the many-body regime. I would write the citation around those two things.
statement.case_against: The reservation I weigh most heavily is still that this is a measurement achievement, and my own standard is that the discovery comes first and the people second. Every constraint on drifting constants, ultralight dark matter or gravity obtained with lattice clocks so far is, to my knowledge, a null result, and I am relying on memory for how competitive those bounds are, so I cannot say the fundamental-physics payoff has been delivered. The second reservation is overlap: the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for single quantum systems already cover neighbouring ground, and a critic can call this the third metrology prize in twenty years. I think the ensemble magic-wavelength idea answers that, but the citation must make the distinction explicit. The third is that a two-name credit leaves out Lemonde, Derevianko, Takamoto, Ludlow and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups, and the Al+ ion-clock line is a parallel route to similar accuracy. I have not seen primary-literature evidence that any of them has a claim to the concept equal to Katori's, but I have not looked for it either, and a prize committee should record the reasons for exclusion.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the ensemble magic-wavelength lattice is a different physical idea from the 2012 single-ion work, that the statistical gain comes from atom number, and that the citation should say so to avoid a generic 'clocks' prize.
responses.response: You have moved me on overlap. In round 1 I treated the 2005 and 2012 prizes as a serious drag; your distinction between a single ion with a motional problem solved by a Paul trap and an ensemble where the magic wavelength removes the problem and the atom number supplies the stability is exactly the physics point I needed. I now consider the overlap a drafting issue and not a scientific one. I agree the citation should name the magic-wavelength lattice and its realisation and should not mention clocks in general. I also agree with you that Ye's credit must be stated as accuracy, stability and many-body clock physics, since a pure record of accuracy is a later and better experiment, a worry Olsson also raises. If the expert reports cannot support that wording for Ye, I would want the committee to hear it before the vote.

responses.point: Kroll treats the pending redefinition of the second as a reason for timeliness and sees no overlap problem with 2005 and 2012.
responses.response: I still do not give the redefinition of the second much weight. It is a decision by the metrology community about units, and it will happen whether or not we award a prize. What carries the case for me is the redshift measurement over millimetres and the independent agreement of clocks across laboratories at 1e-18, because that is nature answering a question. I would therefore drop the redefinition from any citation and avoid presenting timeliness as the reason. On your attribution wording, I agree that Katori as originator and Ye as the person who took it to the frontier should be explicit, and I would accept your 10^-18 regime phrase in the citation. I remain at the point I made before: if the expert reports show a competitive bound on varying constants or dark matter, that strengthens the case, and if they show only null results of modest sensitivity, the case still stands on the redshift and the instrument.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, asks whether the attribution worry about collaborations of thousands that I raised against the Higgs observation applies equally to Halzen and Spiering for IceCube, and holds B029 as his own fallback.
responses.response: It applies in part, and I should say so plainly. For the Higgs, three leadership names cannot represent the decisive ideas across ATLAS and CMS, and I accept your argument that I cannot carry that credit on leadership alone, so I no longer put B026 forward as a configuration I would vote for. For IceCube the problem is smaller but real: Halzen is clearly the conceiver and driver of the project, whereas Spiering's role is longer-term leadership across Baikal and IceCube, and AMANDA and DUMAND are precursors. I therefore regard B029 as an alternative I would support only if the expert reports identify the decisive contributors for the diffuse-flux detection and judge the source identification firm. The difference is that IceCube is a new observational window, so the question is who built it, while the Higgs question is who among thousands made the decisive measurement, and the second is much harder to answer.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene with MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero, argues that speed and breadth of reproduction should offset the field's youth, and accepts B042 as an alternative if the AMO attribution is clean.
responses.response: I accept that reproduction has been fast and broad, and I do not dismiss the prediction and measurement structure you value, which is the structure I like too. My worry is not whether the phases exist but whether they are understood: the pairing mechanism is open, twist-angle disorder complicates the claim that the phases are intrinsic, and a prize committee that waits for nature to settle the mechanism loses little, because the platform will not go away. I also see the credit as less clean than it looks, since Cao and Fatemi, who did the central experiments, and the earlier continuum-model work by Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto are outside your two names. A year or two of waiting would let the superconductivity question mature, whereas the clocks have no comparable open question about the central result. I would not oppose B054 as a later prize; I just do not think it is ripe now.

uncertainties: Whether lattice-clock comparisons have produced competitive bounds on varying constants, ultralight dark matter or gravity, or whether the physics payoff beyond the redshift measurement is still prospective; I am relying on memory and want the expert reports on this.

Whether the expert literature supports a Ye credit based on distinct inventions and many-body clock physics and not mainly on accuracy records, and whether any third person (for example Lemonde or Derevianko) has a primary-literature claim to the magic-wavelength concept.
How much the Al+ ion-clock line and the independent PTB, NIST and SYRTE contributions should weigh against a two-name credit.
Whether the IceCube source-identification evidence (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068) is as firm as the diffuse-flux detection and who is decisive for it, should the committee turn to B029.
statement.conflict_note: No change. I have no known personal or institutional connection to Katori, Ye or any other shortlisted candidate. My mentors and frequent co-authors (Gross, Rubinstein, Van Riet) are not on the shortlist. The black-hole shadow candidate (B047) lies close to my research interests, which I disclosed in round 1, and as I no longer propose it this does not affect my position. I have noted the connections disclosed by Kroll, Olsson and Lindroth and do not consider that they require any special handling for the clock vote.
